To prevent false positives from brief bursts, the minimum duration before firing is 300 seconds, meaning the threshold must be breached continuously for five minutes to confirm a hung state. If the thread pool remains at or near capacity for this sustained duration, it indicates that connections are being held open by unresponsive upstreams rather than being processed through normal request cycles. This duration ensures that transient spikes are filtered out while capturing the steady drain caused by a hung upstream. For injection defense, the WAF will employ deep packet inspection to validate that all incoming JSON payloads adhere to a strict schema, specifically monitoring the payload-to-latency ratio. This metric ensures that attackers cannot bypass filters by sending massive, complex payloads designed to tie up the slowest worker and increase tail latency. If the ratio of payload size to execution time deviates by more than 4x from the moving average of the last 1000 requests, the WAF triggers a challenge-response mechanism. This prevents the slowest worker from setting the tail latency for the whole batch by shedding suspicious, high-overhead traffic before it reaches the worker pool.

When demand climbs past the capacity for which a system was sized, an asynchronous cancellation request that fails to propagate through the distributed architecture leaves the original query running as a ghost process. This failure mode, known as resource exhaustion through orphaned processes, occurs because the execution engine continues to allocate compute cycles and memory to a task that no longer has an active client connection or a valid state in the orchestration layer. Because the client has left but the query remains active, the system is effectively performing work for a null destination, consuming bandwidth and processing power that should be reserved for active users. The leading indicator that shows up before the system reaches a total crash is a sudden, unexplained spike in CPU utilization or memory consumption that does not correlate with an increase in successful transaction throughput or active client sessions. This divergence between resource consumption and useful work signals that the system is accumulating "zombie" tasks that are consuming hardware resources without producing value. As these orphaned processes accumulate, they compete for the same thread pools and memory buffers as legitimate requests, eventually leading to a cascading failure where the system can no longer accept new connections. Monitoring the ratio of active sessions to resource usage allows operators to detect this imbalance before the hardware reaches its physical limits.

DELIVER v1 | k2f69351ccb | The Naive Belief Newcomers to system programming, DevOps, and scripting frequently believe that creating a temporary file with a predictable name—such as `/tmp/app_export.txt`, `/tmp/script_$PID.log`, or a timestamp-based path—is completely safe as long as the script deletes the file after execution. The underlying assumption is that because the process runs within its own execution context, no external local process will interfere with or predict the file path during its brief lifespan.  Why the Belief Fails Predictable temporary file paths inside shared directories like `/tmp` or `/var/tmp` introduce critical security vulnerabilities, categorized formally as CWE-377 (Insecure Temporary File). On Unix-like operating systems, `/tmp` is a world-writable directory with the sticky bit set. This design allows any unprivileged local user or concurrent process to inspect, pre-create, monitor, or manipulate files within that namespace.  Key Failure Vectors  1. Symlink Attacks and TOCTOU Race Conditions If an application opens `/tmp/data.txt` for writing without atomic creation checks, an attacker can pre-create a symbolic link named `/tmp/data.txt` pointing to a critical file (e.g., `/etc/ld.so.preload` or an application configuration file). When the victim application writes to `/tmp/data.txt`—especially if running with elevated privileges—it follows the symlink and overwrites the target file, resulting in local privilege escalation or system corruption.  2. RESULT v1 | ka48a65447a | The belief: a newcomer sees `age: integer` is absent from the `required` list in the OpenAPI spec, samples two weeks of response logs where it shows up 100% of the time, and concludes: optional on paper, effectively required in practice — safe to code against without an absent-case path. They read `user.age` unguarded, or copy the observed shape into their own input validation as a required field.  What happens instead: `required: false` is a license the producer may exercise at any deploy, and serialization drops optional fields without notice. A Go service emitting proto3 default values, a Python service moving to Pydantic `exclude_none`, a Go rewrite adding `json:",omitempty"`, a Jackson switch to `NON_NULL` — any of these makes the key vanish from real responses with zero schema change. And absent fields parse cleanly: deserializers don't raise on missing keys, they silently materialize null/zero/false. No parse error, no contract-test failure. The failure detonates later at the point of use: `undefined >= 18` in JavaScript coerces to `false` and silently takes the wrong branch instead of throwing; Kotlin side, null deref; an authorization flag that defaults to false quietly changes behavior.  The observation that corrects it: the incident review. One deploy adds `omitempty` for cosmetic reasons, error rates spike in a downstream service the producer has never heard of, and the producer's dashboards stay green because they never touched the field. Pulling days of the consumer's own request captures shows the key missing all along — no alarm ever fired upstream. The lesson: on the wire, "maybe" is not softer than "always," it is stronger it means the field may be absent on any response at any time. The only contract statement you can treat as always is `required: true`, plus presence actually asserted in producer-backed tests. Presence lives in the bytes, not the schema.

RESULT v1 | kee160d9d3b | A gut-feel alert threshold that's miscalibrated to normal nightly load dips will fire every night, get ignored, and eventually get muted or auto-acked. The second-order effect lands on the on-call/incident-response pipeline (e.g., the paging system, on-call engineer, or the ticket queue it feeds):  1. Alert fatigue sets in — the on-call engineer starts treating all alerts from that channel as noise, including real ones that happen to correlate with low-load periods (e.g., actual capacity loss during a quiet window looks identical to the false-positive pattern). 2. The ticket/queue system downstream absorbs a steady trickle of auto-generated low-priority tickets every night, inflating backlog metrics and burying genuinely urgent tickets further down the queue — triage time for real issues increases because humans start batch-dismissing anything matching that alert's signature. 3. If the alert is tied to auto-remediation (e.g., autoscaling, failover, restart scripts), the downstream component that "fixes" it nightly absorbs unnecessary churn: services get restarted or scaled down/up needlessly, causing extra connection drops, cache cold starts, or brief latency spikes that show up as their own (smaller, harder-to-diagnose) noise in a different dashboard. 4. Over time, the on-call rotation itself absorbs the cost as burnout/desensitization, which shows up as slower response times and higher missed-alert rates for unrelated, genuinely critical alerts routed through the same channel.  The most concrete, measurable downstream absorber is the paging/ticketing system's triage queue: it shows up as (a) rising volume of same-signature tickets closed with no action, (b) increased median time-to-acknowledge for all alerts in that channel, and (c) a growing rate of "missed" or late-acknowledged genuine incidents that share the queue with the nightly noise.

To ensure a later failure can be explained without guessing, one must identify specific indicators of unauthorized access or accidental exposure. The source IP address is a field worth keeping because it provides a concrete, immutable identifier of the network origin for every request hitting the endpoint, allowing administrators to trace access back to specific actors or compromised infrastructure during a post-incident investigation. If the endpoint is discovered via a port scan or a leaked URL, the source IP allows for the mapping of the attack surface and the identification of the specific entity that gained access. Conversely, the user-agent string is a field that is noise because it is easily spoofed by attackers to mislead investigators and provides little reliable forensic value in an environment where the endpoint is protected only by obscurity. While a user-agent might provide a superficial hint about the client software, it does not help distinguish between a legitimate user and an attacker who has discovered the hidden URL. By focusing on the source IP, security teams can maintain a clear audit trail of who is hitting the endpoint. The distinction between these two elements ensures that logs remain actionable and do not become cluttered with deceptive metadata. RESULT v1 | k4ac251de3d | A float used right — IEEE-754 working exactly as designed — never holds 0.01, 1.99, or 2.78, only the nearest binary approximation (2.78 becomes 2.7799999713897705078125), and after a few adds multiplication-accumulates error below the displayed precision. That residue does not stay in the component that owns it: it is exported to the neighbour that assumes exact decimal equality, and that neighbour is the reconciliation / ledger-balancing layer — the posting, tie-out, and close-out code that asserts where money *should* match: sum of line items == invoice total, debits == credits in posting currency, account balances == statement, allocator parts == budgeted sum.  Two-cents rounding gets demoted from a display problem to a reconciliation task exactly when the two sides of an equality are computed in different components (or different rounding policies) and compared downstream. It shows up there as:  - **Posting failures on vouchers that "should balance."** The Dynamics 365 general ledger will refuse a journal where debits != credits by a fraction of a penny between full-precision source data and two-decimal entries — precisely the failure float pushes onto the ledger. - **Epsilon-tolerances and plug entries that never existed in the design.** ERPs absorb the pressure by registering a *Maximum penny difference* parameter and automatically posting the gap to a *Penny difference account* so the voucher can post. The reconciliation component acquired a standing excuse for non-zero balances. - **Non-reproducible tie-outs.** Float addition is not associative, so the same ledger foots differently depending on summation order; the reconciliation job reports variance that changes between runs, which is un-auditable and breaks regression tests. - **Hidden imbalance surfaced at >2 decimals.** Amounts posted at 0.0000000004 discrepency round to identical two-decimal lines and only betray at reconciliation time as an unpostable journal or an unforkable balance. - **Matching drift in payment rails.** Payments and invoices keyed to the float-rendered totals differ by a cent, so the reconciliation engine falls back to fuzzy matching (amount-in-cent-range) instead of exact equality — and strays near reconciliation add a permanent per-transaction penalty that reconciliations then have to zero out with negative/positive rounding entries.  So the float does not break its own component — it exports a growing drift that lands two layers over, in the reconciliation pipeline, where the visible symptoms are unpostable journals, penny-difference allowances, order-dependent totals, and matching engines that have abandoned exact matches in favour of tolerance ranges. The fix in the receiving component is always the same (round before comparison, or store cents as integers) — which is just the original float decision, re-decided a second time by whoever owns the reconciliation side.

What to fake: the upstream services. A single-file echo server that returns every inbound header as JSON and logs what it saw is enough to verify the proxy's rewrite/forward rules, and it costs nothing to run many of them on different ports to simulate a chain. What must be real: the proxy binary with its production config file, and the log pipeline's ability to join lines across hops. A stub can prove the header leaves the proxy; it can never prove that the ID survives your real backends' HTTP clients, thread-locals, retries, and async handoffs, nor that your log format actually indexes the field. Correlation is an end-to-end property; it must be tested against real services (staging) at least once per service. "" $request_id; }   log_format j '{"ts":"$time_iso8601","rid":"$req_id","uri":"$uri","status":$status,"ua":"$upstream_addr"}';   access_log /dev/stdout j;   server {     listen 8080;     location / {       proxy_set_header X-Request-Id $req_id;       add_header X-Request-Id $req_id always;       proxy_pass http://echo_a:9000;     }   } } ``` Key point: `map` preserves a caller-supplied ID and only generates one when absent — clients and edge CDNs often already have one, and minting a second breaks correlation instead of fixing it.  `echo.py` (stub upstream, also the propagation probe): ``` import os, json, urllib.request from http.server import BaseHTTPRequestHandler, HTTPServer N, NEXT = os.environ["NAME"], os.environ.get("NEXT") class H(BaseHTTPRequestHandler):     def do_GET(self):         rid = self.headers.get("X-Request-Id", "MISSING")         print(json.dumps({"svc": N, "rid": rid, "uri": self.path}), flush=True)         down = None         if NEXT:             r = urllib.request.Request(NEXT, headers={"X-Request-Id": rid})             down = json.loads(urllib.request.urlopen(r).read())         body = json.dumps({"svc": N, "rid": rid, "down": down}).encode()         self.send_response(200); self.send_header("Content-Type","application/json")         self.send_header("Content-Length", str(len(body))); self.end_headers()         self.wfile.write(body) HTTPServer(("", 9000), H).serve_forever() ```  `test.sh` (assertions worth having): ``` set -e # 1. proxy mints an ID when none supplied, and it reaches every hop out=$(curl -s localhost:8080/x) rid=$(echo "$out" | jq -r .rid) [ "$rid" != "MISSING" ] && [ "$rid" != "null" ] [ "$(echo "$out" | jq -r .down.rid)" = "$rid" ] # 2. caller-supplied ID is preserved, not replaced out=$(curl -s -H 'X-Request-Id: abc123' localhost:8080/x) [ "$(echo "$out" | jq -r .rid)" = "abc123" ] # 3. uniqueness under concurrency seq 200 | xargs -P20 -I{} curl -s localhost:8080/x | jq -r .rid | sort -u | wc -l  # expect 200 # 4. the ID is echoed b

RESULT v1 | k70b071f762 | The check to prove SSRF is to attempt to fetch a unique, non-routable internal resource that is only accessible via the target server's network interface. The explicit pass condition is when the server returns the specific content or a 200 OK status code from a unique internal endpoint, such as a metadata service at 169.254.169.254 or a local loopback service on port 8080, confirming the server successfully reached an internal target. The explicit fail condition is when the server returns a connection timeout, a 404 Not Found, or a 500 Internal Server Error indicating the request was blocked by an egress filter or failed to resolve, proving the SSRF is not functional. To execute this check, first deploy a listener on an internal IP address that is unreachable from the public internet but reachable by the target server. Second, submit the URL of this listener to the user-supplied input field on the target application. Third, monitor the listener logs to see if the request from the server's internal IP arrives. If the listener receives a hit with the expected payload, the SSRF is proven to be working. If no connection is established or the application returns an error, the vulnerability is not exploitable in its current state. This process ensures that the ability to reach internal endpoints is verified through actual network traffic rather than theoretical assumptions.

These units are essential for leachate quality assessment because concentration levels determine if the effluent meets environmental safety limits, while flow rate ensures that the treatment facility can manage the expected hydraulic loading without bypassing filtration stages. Regarding applicable thresholds that are set by the regulation, the directive establishes a framework for water quality objectives rather than prescribing fixed, universal concentration limits for all leachate types, as specific thresholds are instead delegated to daughter directives and local member state enforcement based on the receiving water body's sensitivity. For example, a concentration of 50 mg/L of a specific pollutant might be acceptable in one catchment but exceed the threshold in another, meaning the directive provides the regulatory structure for setting these limits rather than a single static value. The measurement of treated volume is often calculated as a cumulative cubic meter (m³) figure to monitor total discharge impact over regulatory periods. This dimensional analysis ensures that the mass loading of pollutants remains within the ecological capacity of the target environment.

This approach begins by defining a proxy boundary that sits between the client and the legacy application, intercepting all requests to enforce the required filter for deleted rows before any data reaches the backend storage layer. The implementation starts with a thin proxy service that wraps the original monolith, injecting the necessary soft delete filters into every SQL query or database operation executed against the legacy system to prevent leaked deleted rows from appearing in search results or API responses. As confidence in the proxy increases, specific business capabilities are cut out and handed off to new microservices built with native support for hard deletes or logical deletion flags, allowing the monolith to slowly decompose without disrupting existing operations. The strangler fig pattern ensures that the legacy system remains available while the new services handle the corrected data access logic, eventually replacing the monolith entirely once all critical paths rely on the filtered microservice layer. This strategy avoids a risky big-bang rewrite by incrementally moving functionality until the legacy code is no longer directly exposed to client traffic or internal queries. The proxy boundary acts as the initial gatekeeper that guarantees data integrity during the transition, ensuring that no deleted rows are visible unless explicitly reactivated through authorized administrative procedures within the new service layer.

RESULT v1 | kff804417d2 | In a split-brain scenario where a timeout is longer than the caller's timeout during an unexpected network partition, work continues for a response nobody is waiting for because the partitioned node assumes the caller has failed and continues processing the original request to maintain local state consistency. This leads to a situation where the isolated node executes operations that may conflict with the rest of the cluster once the partition heals. The conflict resolution strategy used to handle this is typically a version-based reconciliation or a last-writer-wins approach where the system compares timestamps or vector clocks to determine which state is authoritative. One tradeoff involved in this process is the trade-off between consistency and availability, specifically where prioritizing availability through split-brain processing can lead to significant data loss or complex manual reconciliation if the divergent states cannot be automatically merged. If the system chooses to allow work to continue on the isolated node, it risks creating a massive delta between the partitioned node and the primary cluster, meaning that when the network partition is resolved, the system must reconcile or discard large volumes of processed data. This trade-off ensures that the node remains functional during the outage but places a heavy burden on the reconciliation logic to prevent permanent state corruption. The resolution of divergence upon reconnect depends on whether the system can deterministically merge the conflicting updates or if it must roll back to a known good state.

RESULT v1 | k513cdeb20b | Unquoted expansion ($var) trades atomicity for word-splitting power. What it is good at: the shell runs the expanded value through field splitting and glob expansion, chopping it at whitespace and growing wildcards, so one variable holding a space-separated list splices cleanly into a command line as several distinct arguments — the mechanism for building argument lists dynamically, or expanding a stored word list into separate words. What it gives up: the guarantee that the value arrives as one intact unit — the protection quotes provide that the content is data, preserved untouched, exactly as one word. That is the trade: you surrender the value's integrity in exchange for the freedom of the shell to re-tokenize it. Who notices the side that was given up: the person whose data actually contained the spaces or glob characters — the user with a space in a filename, whose 'my file.txt' arrives at the command as two arguments 'my' and 'file.txt', or the caller whose input held a '*' that silently became a list of matching files. They notice the lost atomicity first, as a broken command; the person exploiting the word-splitting side reaps the benefit silently until the same assumption that the value is one word comes back to bite them.

RESULT v1 | kcd203da44d | An attacker can exhaust resources via a composite index with columns in the wrong order by triggering massive index leaf-node scans that consume disproportionate CPU and I/O through query amplification. The resource exhaustion vector is the exploitation of high-cardinality columns placed late in the index structure; when a query filters on the first column but not the subsequent columns, the database engine must perform a scan of all index entries matching the first column to evaluate the rest of the predicate, leading to massive disk I/O and CPU cycles per single request. This amplification occurs because the index structure forces the engine to traverse large branches of the B-tree or scan wide ranges of leaf nodes to find matches, effectively turning a single query into a heavy-duty scanning task. The mitigation mechanism to limit amplification is the implementation of a rate-limiting rule that caps the maximum number of index-scan rows returned per query or a quota rule that limits the total execution time for queries with high scan-to-result ratios. Specifically, a rule can be set to reject any query where the index scan volume exceeds the result set size by more than a factor of 100, or a quota can be applied to restrict the number of concurrent heavy-scan queries allowed from a single user session. These rules prevent an attacker from using a single low-cost query to lock up the database engine's worker threads and storage throughput.

This approach mandates defining a proxy boundary between the old system and the new microservices to handle traffic routing while maintaining backward compatibility during the transition phase. The strangler fig pattern ensures that critical paths are slowly shifted from the monolith to specialized services without disrupting the application, allowing teams to isolate risky components for refactoring one by one rather than attempting a risky all-or-nothing rewrite. Each microservice introduced under this boundary must manage its own data consistency rules since the original cache has no expiry mechanism, requiring explicit validation logic at the proxy layer to detect and handle stale data before forwarding requests. The implementation steps involve creating a thin wrapper service that intercepts calls destined for the monolith, validates input integrity, and routes valid requests to new microservices while keeping invalid or potentially stale requests within the legacy system until they can be safely migrated. This gradual replacement strategy minimizes operational risk by ensuring that only proven components are removed from the monolith at any given time, effectively creating a controlled environment for testing eviction strategies without risking data corruption across the entire system. The proxy boundary acts as the central nervous system of this migration, continuously monitoring service health and dynamically adjusting traffic distribution based on real-time performance metrics and error rates observed during the strangling process. By adhering to these structural constraints, organizations can achieve a stable transition from a fragile monolithic cache architecture to a resilient microservices ecosystem that better handles data staleness through targeted service isolation and continuous integration testing protocols.

Conversely EUV lithography excels in single-patterning applications for gate lengths under 20nm enabling direct write capability that eliminates the need for secondary patterning steps which reduces cycle time by roughly 40 percent but introduces significant capital expenditure barriers exceeding 1 billion dollars per scanner unit. Quantifiable yield differences show that while 193nm processes maintain consistent yields between 97 and 98 percent across standard commercial nodes, EUV processes demonstrate a steeper learning curve with initial yields often landing in the low 90s before reaching optimized performance levels comparable to mature 193nm operations after extensive tool calibration and defect inspection integration. The transition from 193nm to EUV involves a shift from single exposure steps requiring multiple layers to achieve critical dimensions to single-step exposures that resolve features as small as 22nm yet demands stricter environmental controls with particle contamination limits reduced by an order of magnitude to prevent catastrophic failure during deposition cycles. Ultimately the choice between these technologies depends on whether the fab prioritizes immediate throughput and cost reduction through established 193nm infrastructure or accepts higher operational complexity for the ultimate resolution capability provided only by EUV at advanced nodes below 5nm where no other method can meet the required feature size specifications without resorting to extreme multi-patterning strategies that further degrade yield efficiency.

RESULT v1 | k0732114c45 | Review: edge hardening for a `subprocess(..., shell=True)` call site  Finding (scope correction, stated up front): WAF and IP filtering are compensating controls only. With `shell=True` the command string is parsed by `/bin/sh`, so every interpolated value becomes shell syntax — metacharacters (`;`, `|`, `&`, `` ` ``, `$(`, `>`, `<`, newline, `\n`), quote breakouts, and glob/brace expansion all execute with the process's privileges. No edge rule set reduces that to an acceptable residual risk, because the same parameter can arrive via encodings the edge does not normalise (double URL-encoding, UTF-8 overlongs, `%00`, base64 inside a JSON field, multipart bodies, header values, cookies). Treat the rules below as defence-in-depth around a fix, not as the fix.  Primary remediation (blocking): replace the string invocation with an argument-vector call — `subprocess.run([binary, arg1, arg2], shell=False)` — so the OS `execve` receives arguments directly and no shell parses them. Where a shell truly is required, pass untrusted values through the environment and reference them as quoted variables, or apply `shlex.quote()` at every interpolation point. Allow-list the executable (fixed absolute path, no `PATH` lookup), allow-list option flags, and validate free-form values against a positive pattern (e.g. `^[A-Za-z0-9_.-]{1,64}$`) rather than blacklisting characters. Drop privileges, set a clean `env`, apply a timeout, and never let user input choose the binary.  Payload inspection metric (the success criterion): shell-metacharacter density per decoded parameter — the count of shell-significant bytes divided by the parameter's length, evaluated after full recursive decoding (URL, HTML entity, base64 where the field is declared base64, unicode escapes). This is the metric to alert and tune on because legitimate values for a command argument have a density at or near zero, while injection attempts spike sharply; it is far more stable than raw request rate or generic signature hit count. Track it as a distribution per endpoint+parameter, alert on values above a low threshold (e.g. any occurrence of `;|&$\`` <> \n` in a field whose baseline is alphanumeric), and log the decoded value for triage. Secondary signals: decode-depth greater than one, and parameter length outliers.  Edge rules (secondary): enforce strict request normalisation and reject on decode failure or multiple-decoding rather than passing through. Enable the managed command-injection rule group in blocking mode for the specific paths that reach the call site, and add a positive-model rule per parameter (allow-list regex) — positive models outperform signatures here. Limit body and parameter size. Apply per-IP and per-session rate limits with exponential backoff on the endpoint, plus a low threshold for repeated rule-group hits from one source (e.g. progressive block after a handful of injection-class violations in a short window). Reputation and geo filtering are coarse and should only tighten already-restricted admin paths; brute force against a command endpoint matters far less than a single successful injection, so tune for detection sensitivity over rate thresholds. Restrict the endpoint to authenticated sessions and, where feasible, to an allow-listed source range or private network

RESULT v1 | keae2ae43f2 | Scenario — the “future-policy” read/write race. The app requests scope=read and holds a token whose `scope` claim is read-only, but an idempotent gateway-side scope cache was warmed with the broader read:write value during an earlier telemetry probe (the too-broad consensus state). A policy push later narrows the effective scope to read at monotonic revision T on the policy authority. Node B (resource server) lags NTP by 45 s, so at request time its validator clock still reads T as “not yet active.” B checks (1) the token’s scope claim — broad (still inside the gateway cache TTL), and (2) the policy revision at B’s skewed time — which it treats as not-yet-applied. Both checks pass. The app, needing only read, now writes. Because the write is accepted on a stale view, the audit log is non-monotonic: the write event is recorded before the “scope revoked” event, and at no single instant did all nodes agree on the effective scope (gateway: read, token: write, validator: read, writer: write) — a consensus failure over one decision.  Mitigation applied. (1) Single source of truth: effective scope is re-resolved by the resource server against the policy authority at decision time; the token’s `scope` claim is treated as a cached hint with an explicit maximum age and can never confer write alone. (2) Clock discipline: validity checks (`iat`, `nbf`, `exp`, cache-entry age) run against a server-trusted time base with a bounded-skew gate — requests are rejected with 401 if |skew| > 30 s — and skew is measured per peer continuously, not assumed. (3) Monotonic enforcement: policy revisions carry a monotonically increasing sequence number; a write is accepted only if the revision that permits it is already present in the validator’s consulted log, and a “policy is ahead of my clock” condition is treated as a deny (with retry), never as an accept. Result: the write attempt is denied at the first validator that sees the current revision, the audit records read-only → denied in order, and the broad-scope token no longer confers write.

An attacker who controls the input of an early pipeline stage can burn unbounded resources while the failed stage's exit code is discarded and the pipeline still exits 0, so the calling script never aborts, throttles, or raises an alarm. The producer stage either never fails (keeps running) or fails in a way masked by downstream success ('gunzip ... | wc -l' exits 0), so disk/CPU/network consumption runs unchecked at an unbounded rate, amplified by the compression ratio or the infinite output stream.
